{{DISPLAYTITLE:The small trusted core}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/System/The Lean kernel}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Lean is a large program, and large programs have faults. Yet a proof Lean accepts can be
believed without believing all of Lean. This page says why: one small part does the judging, and
everything else only proposes. It names the principle behind that design, the part of Lean that
does the judging, and what the rest of Lean is for.

== A large program with a small judge ==

A proof assistant has to do many things. It reads what a person types, fills in what the person
left out, runs automation that searches for proofs, shows the state of an unfinished proof,
reports errors and keeps track of thousands of definitions and theorems. Each of these is a
place where a mistake in the program could hide.

If a proof were only as reliable as all of that machinery together, nobody could say how reliable
it was. The answer is to separate two jobs. Finding a proof is hard and needs cleverness, so it is
left to parts of the program that may be clever and may be wrong. Checking a proof that has been
written out in full is mechanical, so it is given to a part that is simple and is meant to be right.

The second part is the only one whose mistakes would matter. If it is small, people can read it,
others can write it again independently, and its correctness can itself become a subject of proof.

== De Bruijn's criterion ==

The idea is N. G. de Bruijn's, whose Automath was the pioneer among computer systems for checking
mathematics (see [[Lean theorem prover/History/Automath|Automath]]). He stressed that checking
formal proofs by machine brings a real gain in reliability, because the program that checks them
can be small. Henk Barendregt and Freek Wiedijk, writing in 2005, state the principle under his
name: a proof assistant meets the '''de Bruijn criterion''' when its proofs can be checked
independently by a small program, one that a mathematician or logician can inspect in the usual
way.<ref name="bw2005">Henk Barendregt and Freek Wiedijk, "The challenge of computer mathematics", ''Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A'' 363, no. 1835 (2005), pp. 2351–2375. [https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.2005.1650 doi:10.1098/rsta.2005.1650]</ref>

The criterion rests on a difference between proving and checking. Whether a statement has a
proof at all cannot, in general, be settled by a machine. Whether a given text is a proof of a
given statement can be: the checker only has to confirm that each step follows one of a small
number of rules.<ref name="bw2005" /> A proof may run to megabytes; the program that checks it
can still be short.

Pollack made the same argument in 1998. A simple checker that only verifies explicit
derivations, with no search and no heuristics, is a formal object much smaller and easier to
understand than almost any substantial proof. To believe a proof it accepts, a reader has to
understand the checker, not the proof.<ref name="pollack">R. Pollack, "How to believe a machine-checked proof", in Giovanni Sambin and Jan M. Smith (eds), ''Twenty Five Years of Constructive Type Theory'', Oxford University Press, 1998, chapter 11 (from p. 205); first issued as BRICS Report RS-97-18, Aarhus University, 1997. [https://doi.org/10.7146/brics.v4i18.18945 doi:10.7146/brics.v4i18.18945]</ref> He also recalls a remark of J Moore about
an earlier prover, NQTHM: until one long proof was checked with it, a reader who wanted to believe
everything it had checked would have done better to read all the proofs than its code, because
the code was longer than all of them.<ref name="pollack" />

== The Lean kernel ==

In Lean the judge is the '''Lean kernel'''. Lean's own reference describes it as "a small, robust
implementation of a type checker for the core type theory", written in C++.<ref name="refelab">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0, section "Elaboration and Compilation". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>
Every new definition, theorem or inductive type has to pass it before it is added to Lean's
environment, its table of definitions and theorems; the check is there to catch faults in the
parts of Lean that produced the definition.<ref name="refelab" /> The paper that introduced
Lean 4 describes the same design: the trusted part of Lean is relatively small, and an interface
lets users export their work and write their own checkers.<ref name="lean4">Leonardo de Moura and Sebastian Ullrich, "The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language (System Description)", in ''Automated Deduction – CADE 28'', Lecture Notes in Computer Science, Springer, 2021, pp. 625–635. [https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37 doi:10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37]</ref>

The Lean kernel is kept small partly by what it leaves to others. It does not search for proofs.
It does not work out missing pieces of a term; that is finished before a term reaches it. It does
not check that recursive functions finish: by the time a recursive definition reaches the Lean
kernel, it has been rewritten into a form built from basic recursion principles, which always
finish.<ref name="refelab" /> (See [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Functions that always finish|functions that always finish]].)

== The untrusted helpers ==

Everything else in Lean is a helper. The '''elaborator''' turns what a person writes, with its
notation, its omitted arguments and its overloaded numerals, into a complete and explicit term.
'''Tactics''' are small programs that construct proof terms step by step, some of them doing a great
deal of search. Neither has to be trusted for the soundness of a proof, because neither has the
last word: their output goes to the Lean kernel, which accepts it or refuses it.<ref name="tcl4">''Type Checking in Lean 4'', online book, chapter "Trust". [https://ammkrn.github.io/type_checking_in_lean4/trust/trust.html ammkrn.github.io/type_checking_in_lean4], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>

The difference is visible. Here a tactic, <code>rw</code>, proves that addition can be done in
either order, and <code>#print</code> shows what was actually stored as the proof:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem swap (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := by
  rw [Nat.add_comm]

#print swap
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 prints:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem swap : ∀ (a b : Nat), a + b = b + a :=
fun a b => Eq.mpr (id (congrArg (fun _a => _a = b + a) (Nat.add_comm a b))) (Eq.refl (b + a))
</pre>

The command <code>rw</code> is gone. What remains is a term made of named facts and rules, and it
is that term the Lean kernel checked. If the tactic had a fault and produced a term that did not
prove the statement, the Lean kernel would refuse it, and the fault would show up as an error
rather than as a false theorem.

== What a small core does not settle ==

A small judge narrows the question of trust; it does not remove it. Three things stay outside.
The Lean kernel itself could have a fault, which is why independent re-checkers exist (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Checking a proof again later|checking a proof again later]]).
Some features of Lean let results in without the Lean kernel computing them; they are listed on
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/What has to be trusted|what has to be trusted]]. And the Lean
kernel checks that a proof proves the statement as written, which may not be the statement that
was meant (see [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Stating the right thing|stating the right thing]]).

Barendregt and Wiedijk noted one more tension. Systems in which some equations are settled by
computation rather than by written-out steps strain the criterion a little, since the checker
must then also compute; they judged this acceptable because the basic steps of
computation are themselves simple.<ref name="bw2005" /> Lean is such a system (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Computation inside proofs|computation inside proofs]]).
